title: Unknown teachers
hookLine: the grandmothers, lay chanters and village monks no one wrote down

lines: A CERTAIN MONK. A CERTAIN NUN.
THE QUESTION KEPT, THE NAME LET GO.
THE GRANDMOTHER, THE FARMER, THE VILLAGE MONK.
cards: A certain monk. A certain nun. A certain lay follower.
Some of the old discourses open that way, with no name at all.
Someone walked a long road, sat down in front of the Buddha, asked the question keeping them up at night, and the text keeps the question and lets the name go.
Somebody's grandmother lit the lamp before dawn and taught a small child to put her palms together. A farmer chanted the refuges at a funeral because he knew the words.

teach.h: MARA SAYS GO. THE BUDDHA SAYS NOT YET.
teach.b: Start with the Buddha's last months, in the long discourse on his final passing. Years earlier, the text says, Mara, the tempter, came and urged him to pass away at once: his work was done. The Buddha refused.

He would not go until his monks and nuns, and his lay followers, men and women both, had learned the teaching well enough to live it and explain it to others. Notice who's on that list. Not only the robed.
The householder with a shop and children counts too.

teach.h: A POEM FROM A CERTAIN NUN.
teach.b: In this telling, the teaching was meant from the beginning to travel in ordinary hands. Now the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns.
Its poems carry the names of the women who spoke them, and at least one is credited simply to a certain nun, whose words were kept and whose name was not.

Then a short teaching in the Anguttara Nikaya about two kinds of people hard to find in the world: the one who does a kindness first, without being asked, and the one who knows what was done for them and is grateful.
The Pali word for that second quality is kataññuta, knowing what was done. Put those together and you get today's idea.

Behind the names in this year's story, Nagarjuna, Milarepa, Dogen, Ajahn Chah, stood people no one wrote down: the one who first taught them to bow, to sit, to chant a line. The texts are honest about it.

how: In many Buddhist homes and temples, people remember parents, elders and teachers when they make offerings or dedicate merit, and some temples hold days of gratitude for teachers.

o: teachers who kept their teachings secret
monks who refused to give their names
the ones who taught but went unrecorded

p: urged the Buddha to pass away at once
a poem kept, a name let go
knowing what was done for you

s: in the Buddha's answer to Mara, only monks and nuns needed to know the teaching
he named his lay followers too, men and women, as people who should learn it and explain it.
at least one poem of the elder nuns is credited to no name at all
it's credited simply to a certain nun.
the Anguttara Nikaya calls the grateful person easy to find
it names the grateful person as one of two kinds of people who are hard to find.

games.q: you're the Buddha. Mara comes and says your work is done: pass away now. what do you say?
o: not until monks, nuns and lay followers can live it and explain it.
not until a king protects the teaching.
games.why: in the discourse on his final passing, he refuses until all four groups, lay men and women included, can carry the teaching themselves.

practice: Let someone come to mind who taught you something real and will never be in a book: a neighbor, a coach, a grandparent, the person who showed you how to apologize.
Let their face come, or their voice, or just their hands doing something, and let the thanks be there quietly, the way you'd hold a cup of tea for someone. If they've died, the thanks still counts.

wordCard.voice: Unknown teachers. The grandmothers, chanters and village monks who carried the teaching hand to hand, and whose names the books let go.

orig.note: Pali kataññuta: knowing what was done for you; gratitude.

carryVoice: Your line: no one wrote them down. The names were lost; the teaching still arrived. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16), the Buddha's answer to Mara
Anguttara Nikaya 2.118 (two persons hard to find)
